content: Sodium oxide is a chemical compound with the molecular formula Na₂O. It is commonly utilized in the production of ceramics and glass materials. When sodium oxide is treated with water, it reacts to form sodium hydroxide (NaOH). The alkali metal oxides, represented by the general formula M₂O (where M can be sodium (Na), potassium (K), or rubidium (Rb)), crystallize in a structure known as the antifluorite structure. In this structural arrangement, the positions of the anions and cations are reversed compared to their arrangement in calcium fluoride (CaF₂). In its primary application, sodium oxide is a key component in glass manufacturing. Glass typically contains approximately 15% sodium oxide, alongside other components such as silicon dioxide (SiO₂) at around 70% and calcium oxide (CaO) at about 9%. Sodium oxide, often referred to as soda in this context, acts as a flux, which reduces the temperature required for silica (SiO₂) to melt. The inclusion of sodium oxide in glass production results in soda-lime glass, which has a lower melting point compared to pure silica glass. Additionally, the mechanical properties of the glass are enhanced due to slight increases in elasticity, which arise from the chemical reaction between silicon dioxide and sodium oxide, forming sodium silicates with the general formula Na₂x. Sodium oxide can be synthesized through the reaction of sodium metal with oxygen. When sodium is burned in air, it produces a mixture of sodium oxide (Na₂O) and approximately 20% sodium peroxide (Na₂O₂). To obtain pure sodium oxide, a reaction between liquid sodium and sodium nitrate (NaNO₃) can be employed.
